In 2022, Berkeley PhD student Woosuk Kwon thought he could make Meta's new open-weight model, OPT-175B, run faster in two weeks.

Four years and 3,000 contributors later, that project is @vllm_project, one of the largest open-source inference engines, running on ~500,000 GPUs at any given time.

He and fellow researchers Simon Mo, Kaichao You, and Roger Wang borrowed "virtual memory" from operating systems, handing out memory only as it's needed so each GPU can juggle requests of wildly different sizes. (The "v" in vLLM is for virtual.)

Their first user, Berkeley neighbor @arena, cut its GPU needs in half. Today Google, Amazon, and Meta all run vLLM in production.

In January, the core maintainers founded @inferact and raised $150M to give vLLM a full-time team.

They're hiring across eng, marketing, and devrel in SF and Singapore: https://t.co/DpODvfJWtC

Engineering leaders told Grepr founder and CEO Jad Naous they spend 5 to 20% of their infrastructure budget on observability, and it's buying less and less reliability.

Jad, a former a16z partner, joins a16z's Martin Casado to discuss whether AI can run production systems as well as it writes code.

Grepr sits in a company's log stream, can scan a petabyte of logs a day, cuts observability costs by about 90%, and is building AI agents that use those signals to troubleshoot production issues.

How AI is changing engineering at Jad's 10-person company:
- A data lake feature that once took one engineer about six months took Jad 10 days
- The gap between okay and great engineers on his team "just multiplied 10X"
- He runs 3-4 agent sessions at once, with a "tech lead" agent reviewing every PR

Why running live systems is a harder problem for AI:
- Jad: AI can almost tune databases, but can't yet keep servers running on its own
- Martin: every bit of code doubles the ways a program can behave, which is why humans still own systems
- The real world is messier than AI's training data, self-driving took 20 years and $170B
